lessons.objective: Identify the people whose choices affect the outcome, and the options each has.

body: The people whose choices affect the outcome are the players. Someone in the story who makes no such choice is not a player.
The options each player can choose are their actions.

lessons.objective: Rank outcomes for each person and read the numbers that stand for those rankings.

body: How a person ranks the outcomes is their preferences.
A payoff is a number for how much a player likes an outcome. Only the order and size within one situation matter; payoffs are not money.

lessons.objective: Tell whether choices are made at the same time or in turn, and what each person has seen when choosing.

body: When everyone chooses without seeing the others, the choices are simultaneous. When one person chooses after seeing another’s choice, they are sequential.
What each player knows when choosing is their information.

lessons.workingTitle: When your result is not yours alone
lessons.objective: Recognise when your result depends on another person’s choice, and describe a situation completely.

body: When your result depends on someone else’s choice as well as your own, there is strategic dependence.
Players, actions, payoffs, timing and information together describe the game.

lessons.objective: Find the action that gives you the most against a known choice of the other person, comparing within that choice.

body: The action that gives you the highest payoff, given the other player’s choice, is your best response to that choice.
Compare your options within one choice of theirs, never across their choices.

lessons.objective: See that your better choice can change with the other person’s choice, as when matching or differing is what pays.

body: When your best response is to match the other player’s choice, the situation is a coordination game. When it is to differ, it is an anti-coordination game.
In both, no single action is best for you against everything: your best response depends on theirs.

lessons.objective: Choose the action that does best on average under your stated belief about the other person’s choice.

body: When you are unsure what the other player will do, weight each of their choices by how likely you think it is. The weighted average is your expected payoff.
The action with the highest expected payoff is your best response to your belief.

lessons.objective: Recognise a choice that gives you more against every choice of the other person, checking each case.

body: An action that gives you a higher payoff than any other, whatever the other player does, is a dominant strategy.
To find one, compare your options within each of the other player’s choices. One case is not enough.

lessons.workingTitle: When only one side has a sure choice
lessons.objective: Use the other person’s sure choice to predict them, then respond to that prediction.
Tell apart situations with and without a choice that is better in every case, and spot a choice that is never better.

body: An action is dominated when another action gives a higher payoff whatever the other player does.
Many situations have no dominant strategy at all; then your best response depends on the other player.

lessons.objective: Remove never-better choices one round at a time and check again what is left.

body: Iterated elimination of dominated strategies removes dominated actions in rounds. After each round, check again: an action that was not dominated before may be now.
When one pair is left, the game is solved this way. Sometimes elimination stops with several pairs left, and often nothing can be removed at all.

lessons.objective: Distinguish never worse and sometimes better from better in every case.

body: An action that is never worse and sometimes better weakly dominates the other. This is an edge case: removing weakly dominated actions can depend on the order, so it is used with care.
